blocks: The purpose of this study was to perform an initial study on the application of inspiratory impedance and possible increases in CBFV through the ITD as a countermeasure to mitigate motion sickness symptoms.  To this end, we constructed an OVAR chair with which we could expose subjects to motion sickness provoking stimulus and measure various cardiovascular parameters before, during, and after exposure to OVAR.  The findings of this preliminary study will be used in accordance with a larger and more comprehensive study on the physiological effects of motion sickness and its potential treatments.

Eleven healthy normotensive men and women volunteered as subjects.  Among the 11 subjects, 6 subjects (3 males, 3 females) were symptomatic towards motion sickness during OVAR and were used for this study.  The motion sickness resistant subjects were not used in this study.  The physiological parameters for the 6 subjects are summarized in Table 1.

As off vertical axis rotation (OVAR) has been shown in previous studies (5) to be effective in inducing motion sickness, a rotating chair was constructed and tilted off-axis at 15 degrees for this experiment (Figure 2).  A significant portion of the preparation for this experiment was dedicated to outfitting the OVAR chair to be able to meet the data acquisition needs of our experiment. The OVAR chair was constructed to be self-powered: all data collection and monitoring equipment were housed and powered within the OVAR chair.

The combined facility of the rotating chair and instrumentation was named the Biomedical Angled Restrained Rotating Facility (BARRF) (Figure 6).

After completion of our OVAR chair, we began a randomized, blinded, and counterbalanced protocol with control, where the 6 subjects susceptible to motion sickness underwent OVAR.  Subjects were briefed on the experimental protocol and refrained from caffeine, medications (prescription and non-prescription), and strenuous exercise 24 hours prior to testing. In this experiment, the use of a symptom scale for each minute as an addition to “time on OVAR” was used to quantify the motion sickness symptoms in an effort to better differentiate between levels of motion sickness.  Previous studies have used only “time sustained on OVAR” as the quantifying variable for motion sickness, however this quantification did not differentiate between subjects whose “time on OVAR” were similar though experienced at different symptoms levels (i.e. under previous methods 15 minutes on OVAR with mild/moderate symptoms would be considered quantifiably identical to 15 minutes with no symptoms).³
